Bada! la freccia: Fenton playfully warns Nannetta of his oncoming kiss, extending the lyrical archery duel ('Il labbro è l'arco / E il bacio è il dardo'). Verdi sets their intimate love duet in soaring, flexible lyricism that sparkles within the surrounding comic intrigue.

fatal già scocca.meaning: shoots forth / is loosed (3rd sing. present)

fatal già scocca: Poetic apocope 'fatal' from 'fatale'. 'Scoccare' describes an arrow springing from a bowstring, here signifying Fenton's eager kiss aimed at Nannetta's tresses.
dalla mia bocca: Preposition 'da' combines with feminine definite article 'la' into 'dalla'. The arrow of passion originates from Fenton's own mouth.
Articulated preposition 'su' + 'la' = 'sulla'. Fenton seals his poetic archery challenge by planting a kiss squarely upon Nannetta's hair.

Eccoti avvinto..meaning: here you are (presentative ecco + clitic ti)

Presentative adverb 'ecco' merges with the 2nd-person clitic pronoun 'ti'. Nannetta wittily turns Fenton's combat metaphor around, declaring him bound fast in her embrace ('avvinto', past participle of 'avvincere').

Chiedo la vita!.meaning: to beg for mercy / yield in combat

Chiedo la vita!: Fenton feigns knightly surrender: 'chiedere la vita' is traditional chivalric combat terminology used by a defeated knight yielding to his conqueror.

Io son ferita,.meaning: am (1st sing. present, apocope of sono)

Io son ferita,: Poetic apocope 'son' from 'sono'. Nannetta playfully acknowledges Cupid's dart, confessing she is wounded by his love even while holding mastery over him.
Contrastive conjunction 'ma' introduces the loving antithesis: though she is 'wounded', Fenton is utterly 'vanquished' ('vinto', irregular past participle of 'vincere').

Pietà! Facciamo.meaning: let us make / we make (1st plural hortative/present)

Pietà! Facciamo: Fenton cries for clemency ('Pietà!'). 'Facciamo' is 1st-person plural hortative subjunctive of 'fare', beginning the reconciliation idiom 'fare la pace'.
Completing the phrase 'facciamo la pace'. Fenton leaves the sentence suspended on 'e poi...' with teasing innuendo.
E poi?: Nannetta's prompt question echoing Fenton's words, playfully encouraging him to explain what follows peace.
Se vuoi,: Conditional conjunction 'se' with 2nd-person singular present of 'volere'. Fenton makes his romantic proposal conditional upon Nannetta's consent.

ricominciamo..meaning: we begin again / let us restart (1st plural)

1st-person plural hortative/present indicative of 'ricominciare'. Fenton's playful terms of truce: immediately recommencing the game of kissing from scratch.
Bello è quel gioco: Fronted predicate adjective 'Bello' launching the popular Italian proverb: 'Bello è quel gioco che dura poco' (A game is good when it lasts but briefly).
Relative clause modifying 'quel gioco'. Nannetta wisely cautions that lingering too long in the garden risks discovery by her father and his companions.
Amor mio!: Poetic apocope 'amor' from 'amore'. Fenton breathes a tender exclamation of affection before being forced to separate.
Vien gente. Addio!: Apocope 'vien' from 'viene' with collective singular subject 'gente'. Nannetta hears approaching footsteps and urges a hasty parting.
Rientrano dal fondo Ford, Dr. Cajus, Bar: Ford, Dr. Caius, Bardolfo, Pistola re-enter from the back.
Stage direction indicating the return of the four male conspirators. Their brooding, jealous intrigue shatters the lyricism of the young lovers and resumes their counterplot against Falstaff.
Udrai quanta egli sfoggia: You shall hear how much he displays

Udrai quanta egli sfoggia.meaning: shows off / flaunts / displays (3rd sing. present)

Udrai quanta egli sfoggia: Bardolfo prepares Ford for their encounter at the Garter Inn. 'Udrai' is 2nd-person singular future of 'udire'. 'Sfoggiare' means to ostentatiously flaunt.
Direct object of 'sfoggia'. Boito's mock-heroic phrase portrays Falstaff's aristocratic pretensions and high-flown rhetorical vanity.
Diceste ch'egli alloggia: Ford addresses Bardolfo and Pistola with formal 2nd-person plural 'diceste' (passato remoto of 'dire'). 'Ch'egli' elides conjunction 'che' before 'egli'.
dove?: Ford's urgent, suspicious question demanding Falstaff's precise location in Windsor so he can confront the scoundrel in disguise.
Pistola names Falstaff's headquarters: The Garter Inn ('L'Osteria della Giarrettiera'). Articulated preposition 'a' + 'la' = 'alla'.
FORD A lui mi annuncerete,: FORD You shall announce me to him,

FORD A lui mi annuncerete,.meaning: you shall announce / introduce (2nd plural future)

FORD A lui mi annuncerete,: Ford's speech contains his character label in the libretto cue. He commands Bardolfo and Pistola to introduce him to Falstaff using the future indicative 'annuncerete' with imperative force.
ma con un falso nome;: Ford initiates his deceptive plan to adopt the disguise of 'Signor Fontana' (Shakespeare's Master Brook), probing Falstaff's intentions incognito.
poscia vedrete come: Literary adverb 'poscia' (from Latin postea). Ford confidently boasts to his accomplices that they will watch his trap snap shut upon Sir John.
I catch him in the net.
Hunting metaphor: 'pigliare nella rete'. Both Ford and Alice Ford separately envision catching Falstaff in a net, dramatizing the parallel comedic snares.

Ma... non una parola..meaning: a single / one (indefinite article used numerically)

Elliptical negative command enforcing strict silence. Ford warns his rogue accomplices that absolute secrecy is vital to his scheme.
I do not engulf myself in gossip.

In ciarle non m'ingolfo..meaning: I engulf myself / immerse myself (1st sing. present reflexive)

Reflexive verb 'ingolfarsi' (from golfo), meaning to plunge deeply into a gulf. Bardolfo swears he never drowns himself in frivolous talk ('ciarle').

Io mi chiamo Bardolfo..meaning: am called / am named (1st sing. present reflexive)

Bardolfo cites his own name as a roguish badge of honor and trustworthiness, creating a comic rhyming pair ('ingolfo' / 'Bardolfo').

Io mi chiamo Pistola..meaning: am called / am named (1st sing. present reflexive)

Pistola echoes Bardolfo in comedic parallel, rhyming with Ford's 'parola' to guarantee his own impenetrable silence.

Siam d'accordo..meaning: we are (1st plural present, apocope of siamo)

Apocope 'siam' from 'siamo'. The idiom 'essere d'accordo' formalizes the pact between the jealous husband and the two treacherous rogues.
L'arcano: Direct object of 'custodirem' on the following line. 'Arcano' lends a mock-elevated, conspiratorial tone to their petty intrigue.

custodirem..meaning: we shall guard / keep safe (1st plural future, apocope)

Poetic apocope of the 1st-person plural future 'custodiremo' -> 'custodirem', fitting Boito's strict metrical scheme.

Son sordo.meaning: I am (1st sing. present, apocope of sono)
to be deaf and dumb / utterly discreet

Son sordo: Apocope 'son' from 'sono'. Pistola invokes the traditional idiom of absolute secrecy: being 'sordo e muto' (deaf and dumb).
Coordinating conjunction 'e' links the second adjective, completing Pistola's comic pledge that wild horses could not drag the secret out of him.
Ford confirms universal agreement among the men. The collective pronoun 'tutti' unites Ford, Dr. Caius, Bardolfo, and Pistola in a single conspiracy.

Qua la mano..meaning: to shake hands / seal an agreement

Elliptical colloquial idiom: 'Qua la mano!' ([Put] the hand here! / Shake hands!). Ford binds the conspirators through a physical handshake.
Si avanzano nel fondo Alice, Nannetta, M: Alice, Nannetta, Meg, Quickly advance in the background.

Si avanzano nel fondo Alice, Nannetta, M.meaning: they advance / move forward (3rd plural present)

Si avanzano nel fondo Alice, Nannetta, M: Crucial stage direction introducing the musical miracle of Act 1: the rapid-fire double nonet, contrasting the four laughing women in 6/8 with the five plotting men in 4/4.
Del tuo barbaro diagnostico: Dr. Caius pedantically offers medical analysis ('diagnostico'). Boito crafts Caius's strophe with triple sdrucciolo rhymes (diàgnostico / bàrbaro / òstico / rabàrbaro) to depict his comic pomposity.
perhaps the affliction is much less terrible.
Caius attempts to console Ford by suggesting that his suspected cuckoldry might not be as catastrophic as diagnosed. Apocope 'men' from 'meno'.
Ti convien tentar la prova: It behoves you to attempt the ordeal

Ti convien tentar la prova.meaning: it behoves / is fitting (apocope of conviene)

Ti convien tentar la prova: Impersonal verb 'convenire' taking dative clitic 'ti' ('ti convien', it is fitting for you). Apocopes: 'convien' and infinitive 'tentar'. Caius urges putting suspicion to the test.
Absolute superlative adjective 'molestissima' modifying 'prova'. 'Ver' is poetic apocope for 'vero' (the truth). To discover reality may hurt, but it is necessary medicine.
Così avvien col sapor ostico: So it happens with the harsh taste
Medical simile comparing unpleasant reality to bitter draughts. 'Ostico' denotes an acrid, disagreeable taste. Apocopes: 'avvien' (from avviene) and 'sapor' (from sapore).
del ginepro e del rabarbaro;: Caius cites classic bitter purgatives: juniper berry ('ginepro') and medicinal rhubarb root ('rabarbaro'). Sdrucciolo meter on 'rabàrbaro' rhyming with 'diàgnostico'.
il benessere rinnova: Syntactic inversion: 'il benessere' is direct object of 'rinnova', whose subject is 'l'amarissimo bicchier' in the following verse.
The bitter cup that restores health. 'Bicchier' is apocopated from 'bicchiere' to form a sharp tronco rhyme with 'ver'.

Voi dovete empirgli il calice,.meaning: to fill for him (empire + dative clitic gli)

Voi dovete empirgli il calice,: Modal 'dovete' governing compound infinitive 'empirgli' (archaic 'empire' for riempire + clitic 'gli', to him). Sdrucciolo rhymes: càlice / bàndolo / sàlice. Pistola advises making Falstaff drunk.

tratto, tratto, interrogandolo,.meaning: from time to time / now and then

tratto, tratto, interrogandolo,: Boito uses the rhythmic repetition 'tratto, tratto' (intermittently). 'Interrogandolo' combines present gerund with direct object clitic 'lo' in a four-syllable sdrucciolo cadence.
per tentar se vi riesca: in order to try whether you succeed
Purpose clause 'per tentar'. 'Riuscire' is used impersonally with dative pronoun 'vi' ('se vi riesca', whether you may succeed).
in finding the head of the tangle's thread.

di trovar del nodo il bandolo..meaning: to find the key / unravel a tangled mystery

Famous Italian idiom: 'trovare il bandolo della matassa' (finding the unraveling thread-end of the skein). Pistola advises Ford to extract the key confession from Sir John.
As the willow bends toward the water.
Poetic simile comparing the weeping willow drooping towards running water to Falstaff's natural, irresistible thirst for wine. Sdrucciolo noun 'sàlice'.
Completing the correlative simile: 'Come... Così...'. Apocopes: 'vin' from 'vino' and 'cavalier' from 'cavaliere', producing a brisk tronco rhythm.
Scoverete la sua tresca,: You will uncover his illicit intrigue,

Scoverete la sua tresca,.meaning: you will uncover (2nd plural future, archaic variant)

Scoverete la sua tresca,: 'Scoverete' is the archaic phonetic variant of 'scoprirete'. 'Tresca' specifically denotes a clandestine, adulterous intrigue.

scoprirete il suo pensier..meaning: you will discover / reveal (2nd plural future)

Rhetorical polyptoton pairing 'scoverete' with 'scoprirete'. 'Pensier' is apocopated from 'pensiero' to create a masculine tronco rhyme with 'cavalier'.
Tu vedrai se bene adopera: You shall see whether my art works well
Ford boasts of his cunning scheme to test Falstaff. Sdrucciolo rhymes: àdopera / òpera. 'Adoperare' functions intransitively meaning 'to take effect / operate effectively'.
Subject of 'adopera' from previous line. Ford designates Sir John with bitter venom as 'quell'infame', giving voice to his corrosive jealousy.
E sarà prezzo dell'opera: And it will be worth the effort
Classical idiom 'essere prezzo dell'opera' (worth the trouble / rewarding). Ford believes exposing Falstaff will abundantly repay his anxiety and outlay.
'Discopro' is a literary form of 'scopro' (from discoprire). 'Trame' (literally weavings) evokes the tangled web of Falstaff's seductive schemes.
Se su lui volgo il ridicolo: If upon him I turn ridicule
Sdrucciolo rhymes: ridìcolo / perìcolo. Ford intends to turn public derision back against Falstaff to cleanse his own wounded vanity.
we shall not have sweated in vain.

non avrem sudato invan..meaning: we shall have (1st plural future, apocope of avremo)

Double apocope: 'avrem' (from avremo) and 'invan' (from invano). 'Sudare' metaphorically signifies strenuous labor.
S'io mi salvo dal pericolo,: If I save myself from the danger,

S'io mi salvo dal pericolo,.meaning: I save myself (1st sing. present reflexive)

S'io mi salvo dal pericolo,: Reflexive verb 'salvarsi'. Ford views Sir John's attempted seduction as an existential threat to his household dignity.
Tuscan proverb: 'l'angue morde il cerretano' (the snake bites the snake-charmer / the trickster is bitten by his own reptile). Apocope 'cerretan' rhymes with 'invan'.

Messer Ford, un infortunio.meaning: Master / Sir (honorific title, apocope of messere)

Messer Ford, un infortunio: Bardolfo addresses Ford with feudal honorific 'Messer' (apocope of messere). Sdrucciolo rhymes: infortùnio / plenilùnio.

marital in voi si incorpora;.meaning: embodies itself / takes shape (3rd sing. present reflexive)

marital in voi si incorpora;: 'Un infortunio marital si incorpora'—Bardolfo's comic, pseudo-scholastic euphemism for sprouting cuckold's horns! Apocope 'marital' from 'maritale'.
se non siete astuto e cauto: if you are not astute and cautious
Bardolfo warns Ford to proceed with cunning, setting up the rhyme 'cauto' / 'lauto'.
that Sir John will betray you.
Future tense 'tradirà' with masculine tronco ending, rhyming with 'ingenuità'. Bardolfo maliciously fans Ford's smoldering jealousy.
Quel paffuto plenilunio: Boito's grotesque poetic caricature: Bardolfo compares Falstaff's bloated, wine-flushed face to a 'paffuto plenilunio' (chubby full moon).
che il color del vino imporpora: which the color of wine empurples
Sdrucciolo verb 'impòrpora' (from imporporare, to dye crimson/purple). The wine stains Falstaff's bloated face as vivid as a celestial orb.
troverebbe un pasto lauto: Conditional tense 'troverebbe'. 'Lauto' means sumptuous or opulent. Falstaff's greed would feast richly upon Ford's wealth and gullibility.
Bardolfo ends his strophe urging vigilance: without cunning, Ford's naive trust will be his undoing. Tronco rhyme on '-à' with 'tradirà'.

lo udremo strillar,.meaning: to shriek / squeal / cry out (apocope of strillare)

lo udremo strillar,: In the overlapping double ensemble, Meg Page anticipates Falstaff's squeals when trapped by the women. Apocope 'strillar' creates a sharp tronco beat in 6/8.

e allor la sua fregola.meaning: then / at that moment (apocope of allora)

e allor la sua fregola: Sdrucciolo noun 'frègola' (colloquial for rutting frenzy / lustful itch). Boito captures Meg's sassy mockery as she pictures Sir John's lust vanishing in smoke.
E se i scilinguagnoli: And if our gift of the gab
Tuscan idiom 'sciogliere lo scilinguagnolo' (to untie the tongue-string, to talk incessantly). Boito uses the archaic article 'i' instead of 'gli' before 'sc-' for rhythmic punch.
quell'orco sudar: Part of the clause 'vedremo a rigagnoli quell'orco sudar' (we will see that ogre sweat in rivers). Falstaff is labeled an 'orco'. Apocope 'sudar' rhymes with 'strillar'.
quel bel cinguettar;: Quickly compares the women's animated laughing chatter to joyful bird chirping ('cinguettar', substantivized infinitive). Apocope 'bel' and 'cinguettar'.

così soglion l'ilari.meaning: are wont to / are accustomed to (apocope of sogliono)

così soglion l'ilari: Verb 'solere' (to be accustomed / wont) in 3rd-person plural apocope 'soglion'. Modifies 'comari' (wives) with sdrucciolo adjective 'ìlari' ('così soglion l'ilari comari ciarlar').
Ford, Dr. Cajus, Fenton, Bardolfo, Pisto: Ford, Dr. Caius, Fenton, Bardolfo, Pistola exit.
Stage direction ending the grand ensemble for the men. All five men depart to prepare Ford's disguise as Signor Fontana, leaving the stage to the triumphant women.
Let there be no more wandering about here...

Qui più non si vagoli....meaning: let one wander (3rd sing. present subjunctive in impersonal si)

Alice Ford briskly assumes command: 'non si vagoli' (impersonal subjunctive of vagolare, to roam or wander aimlessly). The women must stop idling and set their plan in motion.
Tu corri all'ufficio: Nannetta commands Mistress Quickly to hurry off on her secret errand as messenger to Falstaff. Enjambment with 'tuo.' on the next line.
Completes the imperative phrase 'all'ufficio tuo' (to your appointed task). Postpositive possessive emphasizes Quickly's specialized diplomatic assignment.

Vo' ch'egli miagoli.meaning: I want (1st sing. present, apocope of voglio)

Vo' ch'egli miagoli: Apocope 'Vo'' from 'voglio' governing subjunctive 'miagoli'. Alice describes Falstaff groveling and whining like a lovesick tomcat. Sdrucciolo rhyme 'miàgoli' / 'vàgoli'.
Alice completes her comic feline metaphor: 'miagolare d'amor come un micio'. 'Micio' is an affectionate Italian nursery/colloquial word for cat.

È intesa..meaning: understood / agreed upon (past participle as adjective)

Alice's brisk confirmation: 'È intesa' (It is understood / agreed upon), sealing the plan to send Quickly to Falstaff at the Garter Inn.
Nannetta chimes in with rhythmic symmetry: 'È detta' (It is spoken / decreed), mirroring Alice's 'È intesa'.
Alice sets the exact deadline for the prank: tomorrow, when Falstaff will be summoned to Ford's house between two and three.
Quickly enthusiastically accepts the commission with double affirmation, ready to deploy her reverent 'Reverenza!' bows the next morning.
Alice bids farewell to Meg Page. 'Buon dì' uses the poetic term 'dì' (from Latin dies).
Nannetta,: Mistress Quickly turns to Alice's young daughter Nannetta with warm maternal affection.
Quickly concludes her parting greeting to Nannetta: 'buon dì'.
Nannetta bids cheerful farewell to the departing conspirators.
Meg Page's merry parting reply as the women prepare to disperse.
Vedrai che quell'epa: You shall see that that belly
Boito borrows the visceral Dantean term 'epa' (paunch/guts, Inferno XXV). Alice initiates the ecstatic concluding ostinato about Falstaff's belly.
terribile e tronfia: Adjectives describing Falstaff's monstrous paunch. 'Tronfio' denotes vanity puffed up to bursting proportions.

si gonfia..meaning: swells / puffs up (3rd sing. present reflexive)

Present reflexive of 'gonfiarsi'. Alice sets off the mounting vocal excitement with rapid staccato syllables.
Meg joins Alice in doubling the motif 'Si gonfia', increasing dynamic intensity as their laughter mounts.
It swells up and then bursts.
All four women erupt in unison: 'Si gonfia e poi crepa' (It swells and then it bursts!). 'Crepare' is vivid, colloquial vernacular for popping or bursting under pressure.
«But my face shall shine upon him»...
Alice quotes Falstaff's ridiculous love letter back at him in a glorious, mocking operatic parody: 'Ma il viso mio su lui risplenderà'. Verdi gives her a soaring bel canto phrase.
...«come una stella sull'immensità.»: ...«like a star upon the boundless expanse.»
The other women join Alice on the grand mock-sublime climax: Falstaff wrote that her beauty would shine upon his vast body like a star upon immensity. Tronco rhyme on '-à'.
They take their leave and move off laughing.

Si accomiatano e s'allontanano ridendo..meaning: they take leave / bid farewell (3rd plural present reflexive)
they move away / depart (3rd plural present reflexive)

Final stage direction of Act 1 Scene 2. The merry wives depart laughing merrily ('ridendo'), having established their moral and intellectual superiority over both the lecherous Falstaff and the suspiciously jealous men.
